(4) Charge liquidated damages, as provided in the rental agreement, or an early termination fee to the tenant if the landlord and tenant have agreed to liquidated damages or an early termination fee, if the amount does not exceed 2 months’ rent, and if, in the case of an early termination fee, the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination. This remedy is available only if the tenant and the landlord, at the time the rental agreement was made, indicated acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee. The tenant must indicate acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement containing a provision in substantially the following form: ☐ I agree, as provided in the rental agreement, to pay $ (an amount that does not exceed 2 months’ rent) as liquidated damages or an early termination fee if I elect to terminate the rental agreement, and the landlord waives the right to seek additional rent beyond the month in which the landlord retakes possession. ☐ I do not agree to liquidated damages or an early termination fee, and I acknowledge that the landlord may seek damages as provided by law. (a) In addition to liquidated damages or an early termination fee, the landlord is entitled to the rent and other charges accrued through the end of the month in which the landlord retakes possession of the dwelling unit ...

83.575 Termination of tenancy with specific duration. — (1) A rental agreement with a specific duration may contain a provision requiring the tenant to notify the landlord within a specified period before vacating the premises at the end of the rental agreement, if such provision also requires the landlord to notify the tenant in a manner prescribed by s. 83.56 (4) within such notice period if the rental agreement will not be renewed. A rental agreement may not require less than 30 days’ notice or more than 60 days’ notice from either the tenant or the landlord. (2) A rental agreement with a specific duration may provide that if a tenant fails to give the required notice before vacating the premises at the end of the rental agreement, the tenant may be liable for liquidated damages as specified in the rental agreement if the landlord provides written notice to the tenant specifying the tenant’s obligations under the notification provision contained in the rental agreement and the date the rental agreement is terminated. The landlord must provide such written notice to the tenant in a manner prescribed by s. 83.56 (4) within 15 days before the start of the notification period contained in the rental agreement. The written notice must list all fees, penalties, and other charges applicable to the tenant under this subsection. (3) If the tenant remains on the premises with the permission of the landlord after the rental agreement has terminated and fails to give notice required ...
(b) This subsection does not apply if the breach is failure to give notice as provided in s. 83.575 .

(1) If the court as a matter of law finds a rental agreement or any provision of a rental agreement to have been unconscionable at the time it was made, the court may refuse to enforce the rental agreement, enforce the remainder of the rental agreement without the unconscionable provision, or so limit the application of any unconscionable provision as to avoid any unconscionable result.

11. NOTICE AT THE END OF THE TERM. Tenant shall give Landlord at least 60 days' written notice before moving out at the end of the term. Landlord shall give Tenant at least 60 days' written notice, delivered as the law provides, if this lease will not be renewed.

answer:
Yes, you can end it by giving your landlord written notice. For a month-to-month tenancy, the notice has to come at least 30 days before the end of a rent period. To move out at the end of April (April 30, 2026), your notice has to be delivered by March 31, 2026. That date has not passed yet. Your lease says to hand the notice to the office or send it by certified mail. Hand delivery is the safest way, because the delivery day is then clear. Put your forwarding address in the same notice.

How will you get the notice to the landlord: by hand at the office, or by certified mail?

DETAILS

### Is a notice needed, and how early?
- Your lease runs month to month (lease §3). It sets no special notice rule for ending it, so the statute decides.
- Fla. Stat. 83.57 says a tenancy without a set end date "may be terminated by either party giving written notice." For month to month, that is "not less than 30 days' notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)).
- You confirmed that your rent period ends April 30, 2026. Counting back 30 days gives March 31, 2026. Today is March 20, so there is still time.
- If you miss March 31, a notice would not end the tenancy on April 30. It would end it at the end of the next rent period instead.

### How must the notice be delivered?
- Section 83.56(4) says delivery is "by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505, or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence."
- Your lease §7 is narrower. Notices to the landlord must be "delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, Gainesville, Florida 32608, or sent there by certified mail."
- Your lease §8 says you and the landlord have not agreed to use e-mail for notices. A text, portal message, or e-mail is therefore a risky way to give this notice.
- If you mail the notice, it is not settled which day counts. One reading is that the day you mail it counts. The other is that the day it reaches the landlord counts. Hand delivery avoids that question. If you do mail it, send it well before March 31.

### Is there a second notice for moving out?
- Yes. Section 83.49(5) says a month-to-month tenant who moves out must give "at least 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery" before leaving. That notice "must include the address where the tenant may be reached."
- For an April 30 move-out, that notice is due by April 23, 2026. That date has not passed.
- One written notice can cover both. It should say you are ending the tenancy and moving out on April 30, 2026. It should include your forwarding address. Deliver it by hand or by certified mail before March 31, and it meets the 30-day rule and the 7-day rule.
- Missing the 7-day notice does not cost you your right to the deposit (83.49(5)). It only relieves the landlord of the deposit-claim notice deadline in 83.49(3)(a).

### What does the lease require at move-out?
- Lease §6 says to "leave the apartment clean and empty, return all keys to the office, and give Landlord a forwarding address in writing." Your notice can cover the forwarding address.
- Keep a copy of the notice. If you hand it in, ask for a signed and dated receipt. If you mail it, keep the certified-mail receipt.

tool_calls.result:
Loaded lease_ending. Its instructions:

# Lease ending

Rests on 83.575 (a set end date), 83.57 and 83.46 (no set end date), 83.58, 83.59, and 83.67 (staying on, no lockout), 83.56 and 83.505 (delivering notices), 83.49 (the 7 days' notice, the deposit), 83.595 and 83.45 (limits on charges), 83.43 and 83.64 (good faith, retaliation), 83.60 (if sued), 83.47, 83.55, and 83.48 (void clauses, damages, attorney fees), and 83.5615 (foreclosure). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes"). Every point marked not settled gets both readings, and you choose neither.

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- The tenant wants to move out well before the end date: load wants_to_leave_early.
- The landlord's notice names something the tenant did: load notice_received_violation.
- A higher rent comes with the renewal: load rent_increased too.
- After the move, the deposit: load deposit_not_returned.
- A new owner after a foreclosure says to leave: 83.5615 calls for a notice "at least 90 days before the effective date of the notice" (83.5615(2)(a)) and protects a bona fide lease's remaining term, with limits (83.5615(2)(b)). Its note says it takes effect upon the repeal of a federal act, and the stored text does not say whether that has happened; say this needs checking.

## What the lease adds

Read the whole lease, addenda included, for: the end date; any notice before leaving at the end; any notice from the landlord; any charge for missing a notice; renewal; staying after the end; how notices go; and what move-out requires. Quote each clause and cite it.

A clause that renews the lease if no notice is given: say what it says. Whether option 1's conditions for a charge reach it is not settled. One: it is a way of charging for a missed notice, so the landlord's own notice is needed first. The other: a renewal is not a charge, and 83.575(2) speaks only of liquidated damages, so the clause stands.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- lease_end_date: the date a set term ends. period_end: with no set end date, the last day of the rent period they ask about. next_period_end: the last day of the rent period after that.
- planned_move_out: the date they plan to leave.
- tenant_notice_delivered: the date their notice reached the landlord, and how it went.
- landlord_notice_delivered: the date a paper from the landlord about the end reached them, how it came, and what it lists. If mailed or left at the door, landlord_notice_sent: the date it was mailed or left.
- permission: what the landlord has said or done about their staying, and whether it is in writing. rent_after_end: any rent paid or taken for a time after the end.
- eviction_filed: whether a case has been filed, and whether they were served. complaint_date: the date of any complaint before the landlord acted, and what it was.

## Which kind of tenancy

- **A set end date:** 83.575. Options 1 to 3, and "When the landlord will not renew".
- **No set end date:** 83.57. "If the rental agreement contains no provision as to duration of the tenancy, the duration is determined by the periods for which the rent is payable." (83.46(2)). A home that comes with a job goes by the pay periods (83.46(3)). Option 4, and "When the landlord ends a tenancy with no set end date".
- **Stayed on with permission after a set term:** read the lease's clause on staying. With none, 83.575(3) points to the 83.57(3) notice; see option 2.

Part II names no right to renew.

## How a notice is delivered

This covers a landlord's notice under 83.575, and either side's notice under 83.57. A tenant's own notice before leaving at the end of a set term goes as the lease says; 83.575(1) names no way for it. The ways: "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence." (83.56(4)).

- **Handed over:** delivered that day.
- **Mailed, or left at the door while the tenant was away:** a way the statute names, but not settled which day counts. One: the mailing or the leaving is the delivery. The other: a paper is delivered when it reaches the person. For a landlord's notice, set both landlord_notice_sent and landlord_notice_delivered beside the date. For the tenant's own notice, handing it over or mailing it early meets both.
- **E-mail under the signed addendum:** only with every condition of 83.505(1); then it is "deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)).
- **A text, a portal message, an e-mail with no addendum, or a copy left at the door while the tenant was home:** not a way 83.56(4) names. Not settled whether it still counts because it reached the person. One: delivery "shall be by" (83.56(4)) the ways named, so it is not the required notice. The other: "This section does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). If there is still time, sending it again by hand or by mail meets both.
- **Spoken:** the statute asks for a written notice in these cases. No notice has been given.

A lease clause on notices adds to this: a way that meets both the clause and the statute is safest. Say what the clause says.

## Option 1: leave at the end of a set term

1. **Does the lease ask for notice?** The lease "may contain a provision requiring the tenant to notify the landlord within a specified period before vacating the premises at the end of the rental agreement" (83.575(1)). No such clause: the stored text asks for no notice before leaving on the end date. Say so plainly.
2. **Is the clause one the statute allows?** Two limits, each with its own question. Say what is not settled, and that notice by the date given meets both readings.
   - The length: "A rental agreement may not require less than 30 days’ notice or more than 60 days’ notice from either the tenant or the landlord." (83.575(1)). A clause outside it: not settled what follows. One: the statute does not rewrite such a clause, so no notice is owed under it. The other: a clause is void only "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) takes away what part II gives, so it stands at the limit. Over 60 days: the date is count_days(lease_end_date, -60). Under 30 days: count_days(lease_end_date, -30).
   - The landlord's half: the clause must also require "the landlord to notify the tenant in a manner prescribed by s. 83.56 (4) within such notice period if the rental agreement will not be renewed." (83.575(1)). A clause without it: not settled what follows. One: the statute allows the clause only "if such provision also requires" (83.575(1)) that, so no notice is owed under it. The other: the statute does not say the tenant's promise falls away, so it still binds. The date is the lease's own.
3. **The last day.** If the clause gives a number of days N: count_days(lease_end_date, -N). If it is in months, give the lease's words; the tool counts days only.

Leaving before the last day of the term: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (83.49(5)), a tenant leaving "before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement" (83.49(5)) gives the 7 days' notice: count_days(planned_move_out, -7), in writing, by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address where the tenant can be reached (83.49(5)). Read the lease for a clause on notice before leaving. Rent through the end date is still owed under the lease.

**What missing the notice costs.** A lease "may provide that if a tenant fails to give the required notice before vacating the premises at the end of the rental agreement, the tenant may be liable for liquidated damages as specified in the rental agreement" (83.575(2)). All of these must be met for that charge:

1. **The tenant missed a required notice.** They gave it in time, or the clause falls under step 2's limits: say so, with step 2's readings.
2. **The lease sets the charge.** No charge in the lease: this part does not apply.
3. **The landlord sent its own written notice first,** "specifying the tenant’s obligations under the notification provision contained in the rental agreement and the date the rental agreement is terminated." (83.575(2)), and it "must list all fees, penalties, and other charges applicable to the tenant under this subsection." (83.575(2)). No such notice, or one that leaves any of these out: not met, and the charge is not owed. Say so plainly.
4. **Delivered a way the statute names** (see "How a notice is delivered").
5. **In time.** "within 15 days before the start of the notification period contained in the rental agreement." (83.575(2)). The start: count_days(lease_end_date, -N). Fifteen days before it: count_days(lease_end_date, -(N+15)); pass the sum as one number. What the words ask is not settled. One: the notice must come during the 15 days that end when the period starts, not earlier. The other: it must come no later than 15 days before the period starts, and earlier is also in time. Set the date it came beside both dates:
   - On the earlier date: it meets both. Say so plainly.
   - Between the two: it meets only the first reading.
   - Before the earlier date: it meets only the second reading.
   - After the start: it meets neither, and the charge is not owed. Say so plainly.

The limit on fees for leaving early does not apply here: 83.595(4) "does not apply if the breach is failure to give notice as provided in s. 83.575 ." (83.595(4)(b)). Do not apply its two months' rent limit or its separate addendum to this charge. Part II sets no number for this charge; a court may refuse or limit an "unconscionable" (83.45(1)) clause, and that is for a court. Apart from this charge, a landlord may claim damages for a failure to follow the lease (83.55); amounts are outside this tool.

Moving out: read what the lease requires. Any claim on the deposit goes through the deposit steps; load deposit_not_returned after the move.

## Option 2: stay on with the landlord's agreement

A new lease or a written agreement says what the rent and the term are. Read the lease's clause on staying and what it requires. "If the tenant remains on the premises with the permission of the landlord after the rental agreement has terminated and fails to give notice required under s. 83.57 (3), the tenant is liable to the landlord for an additional 1 month’s rent." (83.575(3)). So a tenant who stays with permission gives option 4's notice when they leave. Say so. Asking the landlord for its answer in writing settles what permission there is.

## Option 3: stay without permission

Say the risk plainly. A tenant who "holds over and continues in possession of the dwelling unit or any part thereof after the expiration of the rental agreement without the permission of the landlord" (83.58) can be sued for possession (83.58), and "The landlord may also recover double the amount of rent due on the dwelling unit, or any part thereof, for the period during which the tenant refuses to surrender possession." (83.58). Do not total it. For a tenancy ended by a notice under 83.57, whether it has reached its "expiration" (83.58) is not settled. One: a tenancy ended by proper notice has expired, so double rent can apply. The other: expiration means the end of a term, and 83.57 speaks of a tenancy "terminated" (83.57).

But the end date does not put them out by itself: "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)). The landlord "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)), changing the locks included, and if it does or cuts a utility it is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months’ rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney’s fees." (83.67(6)).

What counts as permission, when the landlord said nothing or took rent for a time after the end, is not settled. One: taking rent for that time is permission, since a landlord that "accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant" (83.56(5)(a)) gives up acting on it. Then 83.58 does not apply, and 83.575(3) and option 4's notice do. The other: permission must be given, and taking rent alone does not change a tenant who holds over, since the same sentence leaves open "any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)). Set what the landlord did and any lease clause on consent beside both. Getting the landlord's answer in writing settles it either way.

## Option 4: end a tenancy with no set end date

"A tenancy without a specific duration, as defined in s. 83.46 (2) or (3), may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4)" (83.57). No reason is named. The notice, by rent period: year to year, 60 days before the end of the year's period (83.57(1)); quarter to quarter, 30 days (83.57(2)); month to month, "not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)); week to week, 7 days (83.57(4)).

1. **The last day.** Month to month: count_days(period_end, -30). If that has passed, the same notice works for the next period: count_days(next_period_end, -30). For another rent period, use its number of days.
2. **Written, and delivered a way the statute names** (see "How a notice is delivered").
3. **The 7 days' notice too.** "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (83.49(5)), it also applies to "any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year" (83.49(5)). It must be written, by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address, at least 7 days before leaving: count_days(planned_move_out, -7). Read the lease for a clause on notice before leaving. One notice by hand or certified mail, with the address, in time for both, meets both. Missing it "relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)).

A tenant who stayed on with permission after a set term and misses the 83.57(3) notice owes the extra month's rent (83.575(3)). For a tenancy that was month to month from the start, that is not settled. One: (3) names the month-to-month notice, so it applies. The other: the section is about a tenancy "with specific duration" (83.575), so it does not.

## When the landlord will not renew

The tenant has a set end date and the landlord says it will not renew. Part II names no reason it must give.

- **The lease has a notice clause with the landlord's half.** The last day for the landlord: count_days(lease_end_date, -N). If the clause is outside the limit, set the notice beside the lease's date and the limit's, as in option 1. If it is in months, give the lease's words. In a named way, on or before the last day: met, and the lease ends on its date. Say so plainly. Late, or not in a named way: what follows is not settled. One: the lease still ends on its date by its own words, and the landlord's miss is a failure of the lease, for damages at most (83.55). The other: the clause makes the landlord's notice the way a lease is not renewed, so without it the landlord cannot hold the tenant to the end date. Say what the lease says about renewal.
- **The lease has no such clause.** The stored text asks for no notice from the landlord before a set term ends. Say so plainly.
- Either way, see option 3 for staying, and "After a complaint" below.

## When the landlord ends a tenancy with no set end date

Set the landlord's notice beside option 4's rule. Month to month: count_days(period_end, -30), with period_end the last day of the rent period holding the date the notice names. If it was mailed or left at the door, use both dates, as "How a notice is delivered" says.

- **Written, in a named way, on or before that date:** met, and the tenancy ends at period_end. Say so plainly, and go to option 3 for staying.
- **Too late for that period, or naming a date that is not the end of a rent period:** it does not meet the rule for that date. Say so plainly. Whether it works for a later period is not settled. One: it is still written notice, so if it came by count_days(next_period_end, -30) the tenancy can end at next_period_end. The other: it names an end the statute does not allow, so it is not the required notice, and the landlord must give a new one.
- **By text, by portal, or spoken:** see "How a notice is delivered".

Whichever it is, say not to ignore it, and that the landlord still needs a court case (option 3).

## After a complaint

"It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Not renewing, or giving 83.57's notice, is not named there. Whether either is covered by itself is not settled. One: it is a step toward the action the rule names, so it is covered. The other: the rule lists the landlord's acts, and this is not one.

A tenant sued for possession can raise it as a defense (83.64(2)). The examples of what is protected include a complaint to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)), a tenant organization (83.64(1)(b)), and a complaint under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)), and they are only examples (83.64(1)). The tenant must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)), and "“Good faith” means honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned." (83.43(8)). They must be treated differently (83.64(4)), and the landlord must have acted primarily to retaliate, which is for a court.

It falls away "if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)), whose examples include "violation of the terms of this chapter." (83.64(3)). Whether staying after the end is that kind of violation is not settled. One: holding over without permission is what 83.58 addresses, so it is good cause. The other: that would leave the defense nothing to do whenever a lease has ended. Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## If the landlord sues

Say this first when a case has been filed. "In an action by the landlord for possession of a dwelling unit, if the tenant interposes any defense other than payment, including, but not limited to, the defense of a defective 3-day notice, the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing thereon." (83.60(2)). A motion needs papers showing why the amount is wrong (83.60(2)). A tenant with subsidized rent deposits only their own share (83.60(2)). Give the 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them; "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). The winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying a lease's notice clause binds the tenant without checking the landlord's half and the 30 to 60 days.
- Saying a tenant owes the charge for missing a notice without every condition of 83.575(2), or applying 83.595(4)'s limits to it.
- Saying the tenant must be out on the end date, or that the landlord may then remove them without a court case.
- Stating double rent as owed while what the landlord said or did leaves permission in doubt, or applying 83.575(3) with no permission.
- Applying 83.57's 30 days to a set term still running, or treating a late notice as good for the date it names.
- Saying part II gives a right to renew, or requires a reason for not renewing.
- Giving a calendar date for the 5 days in 83.60(2).
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

tool_calls.result: 83.57 Termination of tenancy without specific term. — A tenancy without a specific duration, as defined in s. 83.46 (2) or (3), may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4), as follows: (1) When the tenancy is from year to year, by giving not less than 60 days’ notice prior to the end of any annual period; (2) When the tenancy is from quarter to quarter, by giving not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any quarterly period; (3) When the tenancy is from month to month, by giving not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period; and (4) When the tenancy is from week to week, by giving not less than 7 days’ notice prior to the end of any weekly period. History. — s. 2, ch. 73-330; s. 3, ch. 81-190; s. 15, ch. 83-217; s. 2, ch. 2023-314.

tool_calls.result: 83.49 Deposit money or advance rent; duty of landlord and tenant. — (1) Whenever money is deposited or advanced by a tenant on a rental agreement as security for performance of the rental agreement or as advance rent for other than the next immediate rental period, the landlord or the landlord’s agent shall either: (a) Hold the total amount of such money in a separate non-interest-bearing account in a Florida financial institution for the benefit of the tenant or tenants. The landlord shall not commingle such moneys with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such moneys until such moneys are actually due the landlord; (b) Hold the total amount of such money in a separate interest-bearing account in a Florida financial institution for the benefit of the tenant or tenants, in which case the tenant shall receive and collect interest in an amount of at least 75 percent of the annualized average interest rate payable on such account or interest at the rate of 5 percent per year, simple interest, whichever the landlord elects. The landlord shall not commingle such moneys with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such moneys until such moneys are actually due the landlord; or (c) Post a surety bond, executed by the landlord as principal and a surety company authorized and licensed to do business in the state as surety, with the clerk of the circuit court in the county in which the dwelling unit is located in the total amount of the security deposits and advance rent he or she holds on behalf of the tenants or $50,000, whichever is less. answer:
Based on what you've told me, you probably don't owe the $2,100. Florida law lets a landlord charge that fee only if the landlord first sends you its own written notice about the fee. You say nothing in writing has come, and the last day that notice could have been sent has passed. You would still owe the rent through July 31. The office can't turn a missed deadline into the fee by saying so now.

DETAILS

### Is the lease's notice clause one the law allows?
Yes, it looks valid.
- Section 11 asks you for "at least 60 days' written notice." Section 83.575(1) says a lease "may not require less than 30 days' notice or more than 60 days' notice."
- Section 83.575(1) also requires the lease to make the landlord give notice if it won't renew. Section 11 does that: Landlord must give "at least 60 days' written notice, delivered as the law provides, if this lease will not be renewed."
- So the lease passes both tests. Both sides owe notice 60 days before July 31. That date is June 1, 2026, and it has passed.

### Does the lease set the $2,100 charge?
Yes. Section 12 says that if you move out at the end of the term without the section 11 notice, you "shall pay Landlord $2,100.00 as liquidated damages." That means a fixed sum agreed ahead of time. Section 83.575(2) lets a lease do this, but only if the landlord meets further conditions.

### Did the landlord meet the conditions for the charge?
No. Section 83.575(2) allows the charge only if the landlord gives you a written notice that:
- "specif[ies] the tenant's obligations under the notification provision" and the date the lease ends, and
- "must list all fees, penalties, and other charges applicable to the tenant."

The landlord must send it in a way section 83.56(4) names, such as mailing it, handing you a copy, or leaving a copy if you are away. Section 83.575(2) says this must happen "within 15 days before the start of the notification period."

You confirmed that nothing in writing has come about the end of the lease.

The timing words can be read two ways. One reading is that the notice had to fall in the 15 days just before the notice period began. The other is that it had to come no later than 15 days before that start. Here that makes the dates May 17, 2026 and June 1, 2026, and both have passed. A notice sent now would be too late under either reading. The office's statement that you owe the fee is not a notice that meets section 83.575(2). A phone call or a remark at the counter is not written either.

### What do you still owe?
- You owe rent through July 31 under section 4 of the lease.
- Section 83.575(2) bars only this liquidated-damages charge. Section 83.55 lets a landlord claim actual damages for a failure to follow the lease. This tool can't say what those would be.
- Section 6 of the lease asks you to leave the unit clean and empty, return all keys, and give your forwarding address in writing. Doing those things protects your deposit claim.
- Whether a court would also find the $2,100 "unconscionable" (unfairly one-sided) under section 83.45(1) is for a court. You likely won't need that argument, because the fee fails on the notice rule.

Loaded lease_ending. Its instructions:

# Lease ending

Rests on 83.575 (a set end date), 83.57 and 83.46 (no set end date), 83.58, 83.59, and 83.67 (staying on, no lockout), 83.56 and 83.505 (delivering notices), 83.49 (the 7 days' notice, the deposit), 83.595 and 83.45 (limits on charges), 83.43 and 83.64 (good faith, retaliation), 83.60 (if sued), 83.47, 83.55, and 83.48 (void clauses, damages, attorney fees), and 83.5615 (foreclosure). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes"). Every point marked not settled gets both readings, and you choose neither.

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- The tenant wants to move out well before the end date: load wants_to_leave_early.
- The landlord's notice names something the tenant did: load notice_received_violation.
- A higher rent comes with the renewal: load rent_increased too.
- After the move, the deposit: load deposit_not_returned.
- A new owner after a foreclosure says to leave: 83.5615 calls for a notice "at least 90 days before the effective date of the notice" (83.5615(2)(a)) and protects a bona fide lease's remaining term, with limits (83.5615(2)(b)). Its note says it takes effect upon the repeal of a federal act, and the stored text does not say whether that has happened; say this needs checking.

## What the lease adds

Read the whole lease, addenda included, for: the end date; any notice before leaving at the end; any notice from the landlord; any charge for missing a notice; renewal; staying after the end; how notices go; and what move-out requires. Quote each clause and cite it.

A clause that renews the lease if no notice is given: say what it says. Whether option 1's conditions for a charge reach it is not settled. One: it is a way of charging for a missed notice, so the landlord's own notice is needed first. The other: a renewal is not a charge, and 83.575(2) speaks only of liquidated damages, so the clause stands.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- lease_end_date: the date a set term ends. period_end: with no set end date, the last day of the rent period they ask about. next_period_end: the last day of the rent period after that.
- planned_move_out: the date they plan to leave.
- tenant_notice_delivered: the date their notice reached the landlord, and how it went.
- landlord_notice_delivered: the date a paper from the landlord about the end reached them, how it came, and what it lists. If mailed or left at the door, landlord_notice_sent: the date it was mailed or left.
- permission: what the landlord has said or done about their staying, and whether it is in writing. rent_after_end: any rent paid or taken for a time after the end.
- eviction_filed: whether a case has been filed, and whether they were served. complaint_date: the date of any complaint before the landlord acted, and what it was.

## Which kind of tenancy

- **A set end date:** 83.575. Options 1 to 3, and "When the landlord will not renew".
- **No set end date:** 83.57. "If the rental agreement contains no provision as to duration of the tenancy, the duration is determined by the periods for which the rent is payable." (83.46(2)). A home that comes with a job goes by the pay periods (83.46(3)). Option 4, and "When the landlord ends a tenancy with no set end date".
- **Stayed on with permission after a set term:** read the lease's clause on staying. With none, 83.575(3) points to the 83.57(3) notice; see option 2.

Part II names no right to renew.

## How a notice is delivered

This covers a landlord's notice under 83.575, and either side's notice under 83.57. A tenant's own notice before leaving at the end of a set term goes as the lease says; 83.575(1) names no way for it. The ways: "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence." (83.56(4)).

- **Handed over:** delivered that day.
- **Mailed, or left at the door while the tenant was away:** a way the statute names, but not settled which day counts. One: the mailing or the leaving is the delivery. The other: a paper is delivered when it reaches the person. For a landlord's notice, set both landlord_notice_sent and landlord_notice_delivered beside the date. For the tenant's own notice, handing it over or mailing it early meets both.
- **E-mail under the signed addendum:** only with every condition of 83.505(1); then it is "deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)).
- **A text, a portal message, an e-mail with no addendum, or a copy left at the door while the tenant was home:** not a way 83.56(4) names. Not settled whether it still counts because it reached the person. One: delivery "shall be by" (83.56(4)) the ways named, so it is not the required notice. The other: "This section does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). If there is still time, sending it again by hand or by mail meets both.
- **Spoken:** the statute asks for a written notice in these cases. No notice has been given.

A lease clause on notices adds to this: a way that meets both the clause and the statute is safest. Say what the clause says.

## Option 1: leave at the end of a set term

1. **Does the lease ask for notice?** The lease "may contain a provision requiring the tenant to notify the landlord within a specified period before vacating the premises at the end of the rental agreement" (83.575(1)). No such clause: the stored text asks for no notice before leaving on the end date. Say so plainly.
2. **Is the clause one the statute allows?** Two limits, each with its own question. Say what is not settled, and that notice by the date given meets both readings.
   - The length: "A rental agreement may not require less than 30 days’ notice or more than 60 days’ notice from either the tenant or the landlord." (83.575(1)). A clause outside it: not settled what follows. One: the statute does not rewrite such a clause, so no notice is owed under it. The other: a clause is void only "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) takes away what part II gives, so it stands at the limit. Over 60 days: the date is count_days(lease_end_date, -60). Under 30 days: count_days(lease_end_date, -30).
   - The landlord's half: the clause must also require "the landlord to notify the tenant in a manner prescribed by s. 83.56 (4) within such notice period if the rental agreement will not be renewed." (83.575(1)). A clause without it: not settled what follows. One: the statute allows the clause only "if such provision also requires" (83.575(1)) that, so no notice is owed under it. The other: the statute does not say the tenant's promise falls away, so it still binds. The date is the lease's own.
3. **The last day.** If the clause gives a number of days N: count_days(lease_end_date, -N). If it is in months, give the lease's words; the tool counts days only.

Leaving before the last day of the term: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (83.49(5)), a tenant leaving "before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement" (83.49(5)) gives the 7 days' notice: count_days(planned_move_out, -7), in writing, by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address where the tenant can be reached (83.49(5)). Read the lease for a clause on notice before leaving. Rent through the end date is still owed under the lease.

**What missing the notice costs.** A lease "may provide that if a tenant fails to give the required notice before vacating the premises at the end of the rental agreement, the tenant may be liable for liquidated damages as specified in the rental agreement" (83.575(2)). All of these must be met for that charge:

1. **The tenant missed a required notice.** They gave it in time, or the clause falls under step 2's limits: say so, with step 2's readings.
2. **The lease sets the charge.** No charge in the lease: this part does not apply.
3. **The landlord sent its own written notice first,** "specifying the tenant’s obligations under the notification provision contained in the rental agreement and the date the rental agreement is terminated." (83.575(2)), and it "must list all fees, penalties, and other charges applicable to the tenant under this subsection." (83.575(2)). No such notice, or one that leaves any of these out: not met, and the charge is not owed. Say so plainly.
4. **Delivered a way the statute names** (see "How a notice is delivered").
5. **In time.** "within 15 days before the start of the notification period contained in the rental agreement." (83.575(2)). The start: count_days(lease_end_date, -N). Fifteen days before it: count_days(lease_end_date, -(N+15)); pass the sum as one number. What the words ask is not settled. One: the notice must come during the 15 days that end when the period starts, not earlier. The other: it must come no later than 15 days before the period starts, and earlier is also in time. Set the date it came beside both dates:
   - On the earlier date: it meets both. Say so plainly.
   - Between the two: it meets only the first reading.
   - Before the earlier date: it meets only the second reading.
   - After the start: it meets neither, and the charge is not owed. Say so plainly.

The limit on fees for leaving early does not apply here: 83.595(4) "does not apply if the breach is failure to give notice as provided in s. 83.575 ." (83.595(4)(b)). Do not apply its two months' rent limit or its separate addendum to this charge. Part II sets no number for this charge; a court may refuse or limit an "unconscionable" (83.45(1)) clause, and that is for a court. Apart from this charge, a landlord may claim damages for a failure to follow the lease (83.55); amounts are outside this tool.

Moving out: read what the lease requires. Any claim on the deposit goes through the deposit steps; load deposit_not_returned after the move.

## Option 2: stay on with the landlord's agreement

A new lease or a written agreement says what the rent and the term are. Read the lease's clause on staying and what it requires. "If the tenant remains on the premises with the permission of the landlord after the rental agreement has terminated and fails to give notice required under s. 83.57 (3), the tenant is liable to the landlord for an additional 1 month’s rent." (83.575(3)). So a tenant who stays with permission gives option 4's notice when they leave. Say so. Asking the landlord for its answer in writing settles what permission there is.

## Option 3: stay without permission

Say the risk plainly. A tenant who "holds over and continues in possession of the dwelling unit or any part thereof after the expiration of the rental agreement without the permission of the landlord" (83.58) can be sued for possession (83.58), and "The landlord may also recover double the amount of rent due on the dwelling unit, or any part thereof, for the period during which the tenant refuses to surrender possession." (83.58). Do not total it. For a tenancy ended by a notice under 83.57, whether it has reached its "expiration" (83.58) is not settled. One: a tenancy ended by proper notice has expired, so double rent can apply. The other: expiration means the end of a term, and 83.57 speaks of a tenancy "terminated" (83.57).

But the end date does not put them out by itself: "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)). The landlord "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)), changing the locks included, and if it does or cuts a utility it is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months’ rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney’s fees." (83.67(6)).

What counts as permission, when the landlord said nothing or took rent for a time after the end, is not settled. One: taking rent for that time is permission, since a landlord that "accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant" (83.56(5)(a)) gives up acting on it. Then 83.58 does not apply, and 83.575(3) and option 4's notice do. The other: permission must be given, and taking rent alone does not change a tenant who holds over, since the same sentence leaves open "any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)). Set what the landlord did and any lease clause on consent beside both. Getting the landlord's answer in writing settles it either way.

## Option 4: end a tenancy with no set end date

"A tenancy without a specific duration, as defined in s. 83.46 (2) or (3), may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4)" (83.57). No reason is named. The notice, by rent period: year to year, 60 days before the end of the year's period (83.57(1)); quarter to quarter, 30 days (83.57(2)); month to month, "not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)); week to week, 7 days (83.57(4)).

1. **The last day.** Month to month: count_days(period_end, -30). If that has passed, the same notice works for the next period: count_days(next_period_end, -30). For another rent period, use its number of days.
2. **Written, and delivered a way the statute names** (see "How a notice is delivered").
3. **The 7 days' notice too.** "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (83.49(5)), it also applies to "any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year" (83.49(5)). It must be written, by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address, at least 7 days before leaving: count_days(planned_move_out, -7). Read the lease for a clause on notice before leaving. One notice by hand or certified mail, with the address, in time for both, meets both. Missing it "relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)).

A tenant who stayed on with permission after a set term and misses the 83.57(3) notice owes the extra month's rent (83.575(3)). For a tenancy that was month to month from the start, that is not settled. One: (3) names the month-to-month notice, so it applies. The other: the section is about a tenancy "with specific duration" (83.575), so it does not.

## When the landlord will not renew

The tenant has a set end date and the landlord says it will not renew. Part II names no reason it must give.

- **The lease has a notice clause with the landlord's half.** The last day for the landlord: count_days(lease_end_date, -N). If the clause is outside the limit, set the notice beside the lease's date and the limit's, as in option 1. If it is in months, give the lease's words. In a named way, on or before the last day: met, and the lease ends on its date. Say so plainly. Late, or not in a named way: what follows is not settled. One: the lease still ends on its date by its own words, and the landlord's miss is a failure of the lease, for damages at most (83.55). The other: the clause makes the landlord's notice the way a lease is not renewed, so without it the landlord cannot hold the tenant to the end date. Say what the lease says about renewal.
- **The lease has no such clause.** The stored text asks for no notice from the landlord before a set term ends. Say so plainly.
- Either way, see option 3 for staying, and "After a complaint" below.

## When the landlord ends a tenancy with no set end date

Set the landlord's notice beside option 4's rule. Month to month: count_days(period_end, -30), with period_end the last day of the rent period holding the date the notice names. If it was mailed or left at the door, use both dates, as "How a notice is delivered" says.

- **Written, in a named way, on or before that date:** met, and the tenancy ends at period_end. Say so plainly, and go to option 3 for staying.
- **Too late for that period, or naming a date that is not the end of a rent period:** it does not meet the rule for that date. Say so plainly. Whether it works for a later period is not settled. One: it is still written notice, so if it came by count_days(next_period_end, -30) the tenancy can end at next_period_end. The other: it names an end the statute does not allow, so it is not the required notice, and the landlord must give a new one.
- **By text, by portal, or spoken:** see "How a notice is delivered".

Whichever it is, say not to ignore it, and that the landlord still needs a court case (option 3).

## After a complaint

"It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Not renewing, or giving 83.57's notice, is not named there. Whether either is covered by itself is not settled. One: it is a step toward the action the rule names, so it is covered. The other: the rule lists the landlord's acts, and this is not one.

A tenant sued for possession can raise it as a defense (83.64(2)). The examples of what is protected include a complaint to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)), a tenant organization (83.64(1)(b)), and a complaint under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)), and they are only examples (83.64(1)). The tenant must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)), and "“Good faith” means honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned." (83.43(8)). They must be treated differently (83.64(4)), and the landlord must have acted primarily to retaliate, which is for a court.

It falls away "if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)), whose examples include "violation of the terms of this chapter." (83.64(3)). Whether staying after the end is that kind of violation is not settled. One: holding over without permission is what 83.58 addresses, so it is good cause. The other: that would leave the defense nothing to do whenever a lease has ended. Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## If the landlord sues

Say this first when a case has been filed. "In an action by the landlord for possession of a dwelling unit, if the tenant interposes any defense other than payment, including, but not limited to, the defense of a defective 3-day notice, the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing thereon." (83.60(2)). A motion needs papers showing why the amount is wrong (83.60(2)). A tenant with subsidized rent deposits only their own share (83.60(2)). Give the 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them; "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). The winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying a lease's notice clause binds the tenant without checking the landlord's half and the 30 to 60 days.
- Saying a tenant owes the charge for missing a notice without every condition of 83.575(2), or applying 83.595(4)'s limits to it.
- Saying the tenant must be out on the end date, or that the landlord may then remove them without a court case.
- Stating double rent as owed while what the landlord said or did leaves permission in doubt, or applying 83.575(3) with no permission.
- Applying 83.57's 30 days to a set term still running, or treating a late notice as good for the date it names.
- Saying part II gives a right to renew, or requires a reason for not renewing.
- Giving a calendar date for the 5 days in 83.60(2).
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

answer:
**Short answer:** No. The text doesn't make you leave by March 31, and your landlord can't force you out without a court case. For a month-to-month tenancy, the landlord must give notice at least 30 days before the end of a rent period. A notice sent on March 20 is too late to end your tenancy on March 31. Whether this text counts as notice at all is not settled. Whether it could end your tenancy on April 30 is also not settled. Don't ignore the text, and don't treat it as an order you must obey.

Has your landlord given you anything else in writing about this, such as a paper handed to you, left at your door, or mailed?

DETAILS

### Is the March 31 date valid?
- You are month to month (lease §3). For that kind of tenancy, either side may end it by giving "not less than 30 days' notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (§83.57(3)).
- Your rent period ends March 31. The count_days tool puts the last day to give notice for that period at March 1, and that date has passed.
- The text came on March 20. It was too late to end your tenancy on March 31, whatever else is said about it.

### Does a text count as notice?
This is not settled, and I'm not leaning either way.
- **Reading one:** §83.57 requires written notice delivered "in the manner provided in s. 83.56(4)." That subsection lists mailing, handing over a copy, e-mail under §83.505, or leaving a copy if the tenant is away. A text is not on the list. Under this reading, the text is not valid notice.
- **Reading two:** §83.505(6) says the notice rules do not "preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." Under this reading, a text that reached you could still count.
- **Your lease:** §8 says notices to you "shall be delivered to the apartment while Tenant lives there." It also says you and the landlord "have not agreed to deliver notices by e-mail." A text is neither of those. That supports reading one.

### Could the text end your tenancy on April 30 instead?
This is not settled either.
- The count_days tool puts the last day for notice for the April 30 period at March 31. That date has not passed.
- **Reading one:** a late notice is still written notice. So if it was valid, it could end the tenancy at the next period's end, April 30.
- **Reading two:** the notice named March 31, a date the statute doesn't allow. Under this reading it isn't the required notice, and your landlord would have to send a new one.
- Both readings depend on the text counting as notice in the first place.
- Your landlord could send a proper notice by hand or by mail before that last day. That would meet every reading. This is a reason not to assume you're safe past April 30.

### Can your landlord remove you on March 31?
- No. A landlord "shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except" through a court case, or if the tenant gives up or abandons the home (§83.59(3)). Your confirmed facts show no case has been filed.
- A landlord may not keep you out by any means, including changing the locks. If a landlord does this or cuts off a utility, it is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney's fees." (§83.67(6))
- If you stay past a date that validly ends your tenancy, the landlord can sue you for possession. It may also claim double rent for the time you stay (§83.58). Whether that double-rent rule applies after a month-to-month notice is not settled.
- The landlord's reason, redoing the unit, does not matter here. Part II doesn't require a reason to end a month-to-month tenancy.

### What if the landlord does sue?
If you are served with a court case, don't wait. If you raise any defense other than payment, you must pay the rent into the court registry, or file a motion about the amount, within 5 days after you are served. The 5 days leave out Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays. If you miss this, you lose your defenses (§83.60(2)).

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.

Its note says it takes effect upon the repeal of a federal act, and the stored text does not say whether that has happened; say this needs checking.

## What the lease adds

Read the whole lease, addenda included, for: the end date; any notice before leaving at the end; any notice from the landlord; any charge for missing a notice; renewal; staying after the end; how notices go; and what move-out requires. Quote each clause and cite it.

A clause that renews the lease if no notice is given: say what it says. Whether option 1's conditions for a charge reach it is not settled. One: it is a way of charging for a missed notice, so the landlord's own notice is needed first. The other: a renewal is not a charge, and 83.575(2) speaks only of liquidated damages, so the clause stands.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- lease_end_date: the date a set term ends. period_end: with no set end date, the last day of the rent period they ask about. next_period_end: the last day of the rent period after that.
- planned_move_out: the date they plan to leave.
- tenant_notice_delivered: the date their notice reached the landlord, and how it went.
- landlord_notice_delivered: the date a paper from the landlord about the end reached them, how it came, and what it lists. If mailed or left at the door, landlord_notice_sent: the date it was mailed or left.

- **No set end date:** 83.57. "If the rental agreement contains no provision as to duration of the tenancy, the duration is determined by the periods for which the rent is payable." (83.46(2)). - **Stayed on with permission after a set term:** read the lease's clause on staying. With none, 83.575(3) points to the 83.57(3) notice; see option 2.

This covers a landlord's notice under 83.575, and either side's notice under 83.57. A tenant's own notice before leaving at the end of a set term goes as the lease says; 83.575(1) names no way for it. A lease clause on notices adds to this: a way that meets both the clause and the statute is safest. Say what the clause says.

(83.58). Do not total it. For a tenancy ended by a notice under 83.57, whether it has reached its "expiration" (83.58) is not settled. But the end date does not put them out by itself: "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)). The landlord "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)), changing the locks included, and if it does or cuts a utility it is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months’ rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney’s fees." (83.67(6)).

What counts as permission, when the landlord said nothing or took rent for a time after the end, is not settled. One: taking rent for that time is permission, since a landlord that "accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant" (83.56(5)(a)) gives up acting on it. Then 83.58 does not apply, and 83.575(3) and option 4's notice do. The other: permission must be given, and taking rent alone does not change a tenant who holds over, since the same sentence leaves open "any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)). Set what the landlord did and any lease clause on consent beside both. Getting the landlord's answer in writing settles it either way.

## Option 4: end a tenancy with no set end date

"A tenancy without a specific duration, as defined in s. 83.46 (2) or (3), may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4)" (83.57). No reason is named. The notice, by rent period: year to year, 60 days before the end of the year's period (83.57(1)); quarter to quarter, 30 days (83.57(2)); month to month, "not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)); week to week, 7 days (83.57(4)).

1. **The last day.** Month to month: count_days(period_end, -30). If that has passed, the same notice works for the next period: count_days(next_period_end, -30). For another rent period, use its number of days.
2. **Written, and delivered a way the statute names** (see "How a notice is delivered").
3. **The 7 days' notice too.** "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (83.49(5)), it also applies to "any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year" (83.49(5)). It must be written, by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address, at least 7 days before leaving: count_days(planned_move_out, -7). Read the lease for a clause on notice before leaving. One notice by hand or certified mail, with the address, in time for both, meets both. Missing it "relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)).

A tenant who stayed on with permission after a set term and misses the 83.57(3) notice owes the extra month's rent (83.575(3)). For a tenancy that was month to month from the start, that is not settled. One: (3) names the month-to-month notice, so it applies. The other: the section is about a tenancy "with specific duration" (83.575), so it does not.

## When the landlord will not renew

The tenant has a set end date and the landlord says it will not renew. Part II names no reason it must give.

- **The lease has a notice clause with the landlord's half.** The last day for the landlord: count_days(lease_end_date, -N). If the clause is outside the limit, set the notice beside the lease's date and the limit's, as in option 1. If it is in months, give the lease's words. In a named way, on or before the last day: met, and the lease ends on its date. Say so plainly. Late, or not in a named way: what follows is not settled. One: the lease still ends on its date by its own words, and the landlord's miss is a failure of the lease, for damages at most (83.55). The other: the clause makes the landlord's notice the way a lease is not renewed, so without it the landlord cannot hold the tenant to the end date. Say what the lease says about renewal.
- **The lease has no such clause.** The stored text asks for no notice from the landlord before a set term ends. Say so plainly.
- Either way, see option 3 for staying, and "After a complaint" below.

## When the landlord ends a tenancy with no set end date

Set the landlord's notice beside option 4's rule. Month to month: count_days(period_end, -30), with period_end the last day of the rent period holding the date the notice names. If it was mailed or left at the door, use both dates, as "How a notice is delivered" says.

- **Written, in a named way, on or before that date:** met, and the tenancy ends at period_end. Say so plainly, and go to option 3 for staying.
- **Too late for that period, or naming a date that is not the end of a rent period:** it does not meet the rule for that date. Say so plainly. Whether it works for a later period is not settled. One: it is still written notice, so if it came by count_days(next_period_end, -30) the tenancy can end at next_period_end. The other: it names an end the statute does not allow, so it is not the required notice, and the landlord must give a new one.
- **By text, by portal, or spoken:** see "How a notice is delivered".

Whichever it is, say not to ignore it, and that the landlord still needs a court case (option 3).

## After a complaint

"It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Not renewing, or giving 83.57's notice, is not named there. Whether either is covered by itself is not settled. One: it is a step toward the action the rule names, so it is covered. The other: the rule lists the landlord's acts, and this is not one.

A tenant sued for possession can raise it as a defense (83.64(2)). The examples of what is protected include a complaint to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)), a tenant organization (83.64(1)(b)), and a complaint under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)), and they are only examples (83.64(1)). The tenant must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)), and "“Good faith” means honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned." (83.43(8)). They must be treated differently (83.64(4)), and the landlord must have acted primarily to retaliate, which is for a court.

It falls away "if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)), whose examples include "violation of the terms of this chapter." (83.64(3)). Whether staying after the end is that kind of violation is not settled. One: holding over without permission is what 83.58 addresses, so it is good cause. The other: that would leave the defense nothing to do whenever a lease has ended. Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## If the landlord sues

Say this first when a case has been filed. "In an action by the landlord for possession of a dwelling unit, if the tenant interposes any defense other than payment, including, but not limited to, the defense of a defective 3-day notice, the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing thereon." (83.60(2)). A motion needs papers showing why the amount is wrong (83.60(2)). A tenant with subsidized rent deposits only their own share (83.60(2)). Give the 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them; "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). The winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying a lease's notice clause binds the tenant without checking the landlord's half and the 30 to 60 days.
- Saying a tenant owes the charge for missing a notice without every condition of 83.575(2), or applying 83.595(4)'s limits to it.
- Saying the tenant must be out on the end date, or that the landlord may then remove them without a court case.
- Stating double rent as owed while what the landlord said or did leaves permission in doubt, or applying 83.575(3) with no permission.
- Applying 83.57's 30 days to a set term still running, or treating a late notice as good for the date it names.
- Saying part II gives a right to renew, or requires a reason for not renewing.
- Giving a calendar date for the 5 days in 83.60(2).
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

answer:
It's not settled whether you owe the $2,100. Everything else the law requires for that charge appears to be met, but the timing of your landlord's letter is a close question. If the law means the letter had to arrive in a certain 15-day window, the letter was on time and you likely owe the charge. If the law means the letter had to arrive by a cutoff date, the letter was late and you likely don't. A court would have to decide which reading is right. You missed your own notice deadline of June 1, so the $2,100 is a real risk.

DETAILS

### Does your lease's notice clause meet the law's limits?
- Section 11 of your lease asks you for "at least 60 days' written notice before moving out at the end of the term." The statute allows notice of 30 to 60 days (83.575(1)), so 60 days is within the limit.
- The statute also requires the clause to bind the landlord to give notice if the lease won't be renewed (83.575(1)). Section 11 does: "Landlord shall give Tenant at least 60 days' written notice, delivered as the law provides, if this lease will not be renewed."
- Your last day to give notice was June 1, 2026. That date has passed, and you told me you gave no notice.

### Does your lease set the charge?
Yes. Section 12 says that if you move out at the end of the term without the section 11 notice, you "shall pay Landlord $2,100.00 as liquidated damages." Liquidated damages are a set dollar amount agreed in advance. The statute allows this kind of charge (83.575(2)).

### Did the landlord's letter have the right content?
- The statute requires a written notice from the landlord. It must specify your obligations under the lease's notice clause and the date the lease ends, and it "must list all fees, penalties, and other charges" (83.575(2)).
- You told me the letter covered the 60-day notice requirement, the July 31, 2026 end date, and the $2,100 charge. It also said there were no other fees, penalties, or charges.
- On what you've described, the content is complete.

### Was the letter delivered in a way the law allows?
- The letter was handed to you at the apartment door on May 20. Handing a notice to the tenant is a named way of delivering it (83.56(4)).
- Your lease says notices to you are "delivered to the apartment while Tenant lives there" (section 8). Hand delivery to you at the door fits that too.

### Was the letter on time? This is the open point.
- The statute says the landlord's notice must be given "within 15 days before the start of the notification period" (83.575(2)).
- Your notification period started June 1, 2026. Fifteen days before that is May 17, 2026. Your letter came on May 20, which is after May 17 and before June 1.
- **Reading one:** the letter had to arrive during the 15 days that end when the period starts. May 20 falls in that window, so the letter was on time and the charge can apply.
- **Reading two:** the letter had to arrive no later than 15 days before the period starts. May 20 is after May 17, so the letter was late and the charge is not owed.
- Part II doesn't say which reading is correct.

### Are there other limits on the charge?
- The cap on charges for leaving early, 83.595(4), doesn't apply to a missed notice under 83.575 (83.595(4)(b)).
- A court can refuse or limit a charge it finds "unconscionable" (83.45(1)). That would be the court's decision, and I can't predict it.

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- lease_end_date: the date a set term ends. period_end: with no set end date, the last day of the rent period they ask about. next_period_end: the last day of the rent period after that.

- **A set end date:** 83.575. Options 1 to 3, and "When the landlord will not renew".
- **No set end date:** 83.57. "If the rental agreement contains no provision as to duration of the tenancy, the duration is determined by the periods for which the rent is payable." (83.46(2)).
