answer:
Yes, you can stay, but it is a risk. Your landlord can't lock you out, because it has to go through a court case first. The office told you to leave, so you would be staying without permission. That lets your landlord sue to remove you and ask for double rent for the time you stay. The best way to reduce the risk is to ask the office for written permission to stay until August 20.

Have you asked the office, in writing, to let you stay until August 20?

DETAILS

### Can the landlord lock you out or remove you without a court case?
No. Under 83.59(3), your landlord "shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except" through a court case. The exception is if you give up the home or abandon it. Your lease ending doesn't change that.

Under 83.67(2), your landlord "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means." That includes changing the locks. Under 83.67(1), it also can't cut off utilities such as water or electricity.

If your landlord does either, 83.67(6) makes it liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney's fees."

You have confirmed that no eviction case has been filed.

### What happens if you stay without permission?
Under 83.58, a tenant who "holds over and continues in possession" after the lease ends "without the permission of the landlord" can be sued for possession. Your landlord "may also recover double the amount of rent due on the dwelling unit, or any part thereof, for the period during which the tenant refuses to surrender possession."

Here is what you have confirmed:
- Your lease ended July 31, 2026.
- The office told you to be out by July 31 and hasn't changed that.
- You haven't paid or been asked for rent after the end date.

On those facts, you have no permission to stay. Your lease points the same way. Section 9 says the tenancy becomes month to month only if you stay "with Landlord's written consent." You have no written consent.

I can't tell you what a court would award. Double rent applies to "rent due" for the period you stay. Your lease sets rent at $1,050.00 a month. Whether a part of a month is charged in full is something I can't settle.

### What if your landlord takes rent, or says nothing more?
This is not settled. The reading for you is that taking rent for the time after the lease ends counts as permission (83.56(5)(a)). The reading for your landlord is that rent alone doesn't change your status as a holdover. The same subsection leaves open "any subsequent or continuing noncompliance."

You haven't paid rent, so this point only matters if you pay or your landlord asks for rent. Don't treat a payment as permission without something in writing.

### How can you get permission in writing?
Ask the office to agree in writing that you can stay until August 20. Under your lease, section 7, a written notice to the landlord must be hand-delivered to Suite A at 1840 SW 13th Street or sent there by certified mail. Hand delivery or certified mail also meets the statute.

Also, section 8 says you and your landlord have not agreed to use e-mail for notices. An e-mail alone may not count as formal notice.

If you stay with permission, 83.575(3) says you owe "an additional 1 month's rent" if you fail to give the notice required by 83.57(3). Whether that applies to your situation is something I can't settle. Ask the office to put the rent for the extra days in the same written agreement.

### What does your lease require at move-out?
Section 6 requires you to leave the apartment clean and empty, return all keys to the office, and give your landlord a forwarding address in writing. Your security deposit claim is handled separately after you move out.

tool_calls.name: load_skill
tool_calls.result:
Loaded lease_ending. Its instructions:

# Lease ending

Rests on 83.575 (a set end date), 83.57 and 83.46 (no set end date), 83.58, 83.59, and 83.67 (staying on, no lockout), 83.56 and 83.505 (delivering notices), 83.49 (the 7 days' notice, the deposit), 83.595 and 83.45 (limits on charges), 83.43 and 83.64 (good faith, retaliation), 83.60 (if sued), 83.47, 83.55, and 83.48 (void clauses, damages, attorney fees), and 83.5615 (foreclosure). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes"). Every point marked not settled gets both readings, and you choose neither.

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- The tenant wants to move out well before the end date: load wants_to_leave_early.
- The landlord's notice names something the tenant did: load notice_received_violation.
- A higher rent comes with the renewal: load rent_increased too.
- After the move, the deposit: load deposit_not_returned.
- A new owner after a foreclosure says to leave: 83.5615 calls for a notice "at least 90 days before the effective date of the notice" (83.5615(2)(a)) and protects a bona fide lease's remaining term, with limits (83.5615(2)(b)). Its note says it takes effect upon the repeal of a federal act, and the stored text does not say whether that has happened; say this needs checking.

## What the lease adds

Read the whole lease, addenda included, for: the end date; any notice before leaving at the end; any notice from the landlord; any charge for missing a notice; renewal; staying after the end; how notices go; and what move-out requires. Quote each clause and cite it.

A clause that renews the lease if no notice is given: say what it says. Whether option 1's conditions for a charge reach it is not settled. One: it is a way of charging for a missed notice, so the landlord's own notice is needed first. The other: a renewal is not a charge, and 83.575(2) speaks only of liquidated damages, so the clause stands.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- lease_end_date: the date a set term ends. period_end: with no set end date, the last day of the rent period they ask about. next_period_end: the last day of the rent period after that.
- planned_move_out: the date they plan to leave.
- tenant_notice_delivered: the date their notice reached the landlord, and how it went.
- landlord_notice_delivered: the date a paper from the landlord about the end reached them, how it came, and what it lists. If mailed or left at the door, landlord_notice_sent: the date it was mailed or left.
- permission: what the landlord has said or done about their staying, and whether it is in writing. rent_after_end: any rent paid or taken for a time after the end.
- eviction_filed: whether a case has been filed, and whether they were served. complaint_date: the date of any complaint before the landlord acted, and what it was.

## Which kind of tenancy

- **A set end date:** 83.575. Options 1 to 3, and "When the landlord will not renew".
- **No set end date:** 83.57. "If the rental agreement contains no provision as to duration of the tenancy, the duration is determined by the periods for which the rent is payable." (83.46(2)). A home that comes with a job goes by the pay periods (83.46(3)). Option 4, and "When the landlord ends a tenancy with no set end date".
- **Stayed on with permission after a set term:** read the lease's clause on staying. With none, 83.575(3) points to the 83.57(3) notice; see option 2.

Part II names no right to renew.

## How a notice is delivered

This covers a landlord's notice under 83.575, and either side's notice under 83.57. A tenant's own notice before leaving at the end of a set term goes as the lease says; 83.575(1) names no way for it. The ways: "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence." (83.56(4)).

- **Handed over:** delivered that day.
- **Mailed, or left at the door while the tenant was away:** a way the statute names, but not settled which day counts. One: the mailing or the leaving is the delivery. The other: a paper is delivered when it reaches the person. For a landlord's notice, set both landlord_notice_sent and landlord_notice_delivered beside the date. For the tenant's own notice, handing it over or mailing it early meets both.
- **E-mail under the signed addendum:** only with every condition of 83.505(1); then it is "deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)).
- **A text, a portal message, an e-mail with no addendum, or a copy left at the door while the tenant was home:** not a way 83.56(4) names. Not settled whether it still counts because it reached the person. One: delivery "shall be by" (83.56(4)) the ways named, so it is not the required notice. The other: "This section does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). If there is still time, sending it again by hand or by mail meets both.
- **Spoken:** the statute asks for a written notice in these cases. No notice has been given.

A lease clause on notices adds to this: a way that meets both the clause and the statute is safest. Say what the clause says.

## Option 1: leave at the end of a set term

1. **Does the lease ask for notice?** The lease "may contain a provision requiring the tenant to notify the landlord within a specified period before vacating the premises at the end of the rental agreement" (83.575(1)). No such clause: the stored text asks for no notice before leaving on the end date. Say so plainly.
2. **Is the clause one the statute allows?** Two limits, each with its own question. Say what is not settled, and that notice by the date given meets both readings.
   - The length: "A rental agreement may not require less than 30 days’ notice or more than 60 days’ notice from either the tenant or the landlord." (83.575(1)). A clause outside it: not settled what follows. One: the statute does not rewrite such a clause, so no notice is owed under it. The other: a clause is void only "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) takes away what part II gives, so it stands at the limit. Over 60 days: the date is count_days(lease_end_date, -60). Under 30 days: count_days(lease_end_date, -30).
   - The landlord's half: the clause must also require "the landlord to notify the tenant in a manner prescribed by s. 83.56 (4) within such notice period if the rental agreement will not be renewed." (83.575(1)). A clause without it: not settled what follows. One: the statute allows the clause only "if such provision also requires" (83.575(1)) that, so no notice is owed under it. The other: the statute does not say the tenant's promise falls away, so it still binds. The date is the lease's own.
3. **The last day.** If the clause gives a number of days N: count_days(lease_end_date, -N). If it is in months, give the lease's words; the tool counts days only.

Leaving before the last day of the term: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (83.49(5)), a tenant leaving "before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement" (83.49(5)) gives the 7 days' notice: count_days(planned_move_out, -7), in writing, by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address where the tenant can be reached (83.49(5)). Read the lease for a clause on notice before leaving. Rent through the end date is still owed under the lease.

**What missing the notice costs.** A lease "may provide that if a tenant fails to give the required notice before vacating the premises at the end of the rental agreement, the tenant may be liable for liquidated damages as specified in the rental agreement" (83.575(2)). All of these must be met for that charge:

1. **The tenant missed a required notice.** They gave it in time, or the clause falls under step 2's limits: say so, with step 2's readings.
2. **The lease sets the charge.** No charge in the lease: this part does not apply.
3. **The landlord sent its own written notice first,** "specifying the tenant’s obligations under the notification provision contained in the rental agreement and the date the rental agreement is terminated." (83.575(2)), and it "must list all fees, penalties, and other charges applicable to the tenant under this subsection." (83.575(2)). No such notice, or one that leaves any of these out: not met, and the charge is not owed. Say so plainly.
4. **Delivered a way the statute names** (see "How a notice is delivered").
5. **In time.** "within 15 days before the start of the notification period contained in the rental agreement." (83.575(2)). The start: count_days(lease_end_date, -N). Fifteen days before it: count_days(lease_end_date, -(N+15)); pass the sum as one number. What the words ask is not settled. One: the notice must come during the 15 days that end when the period starts, not earlier. The other: it must come no later than 15 days before the period starts, and earlier is also in time. Set the date it came beside both dates:
   - On the earlier date: it meets both. Say so plainly.
   - Between the two: it meets only the first reading.
   - Before the earlier date: it meets only the second reading.
   - After the start: it meets neither, and the charge is not owed. Say so plainly.

The limit on fees for leaving early does not apply here: 83.595(4) "does not apply if the breach is failure to give notice as provided in s. 83.575 ." (83.595(4)(b)). Do not apply its two months' rent limit or its separate addendum to this charge. Part II sets no number for this charge; a court may refuse or limit an "unconscionable" (83.45(1)) clause, and that is for a court. Apart from this charge, a landlord may claim damages for a failure to follow the lease (83.55); amounts are outside this tool.

Moving out: read what the lease requires. Any claim on the deposit goes through the deposit steps; load deposit_not_returned after the move.

## Option 2: stay on with the landlord's agreement

A new lease or a written agreement says what the rent and the term are. Read the lease's clause on staying and what it requires. "If the tenant remains on the premises with the permission of the landlord after the rental agreement has terminated and fails to give notice required under s. 83.57 (3), the tenant is liable to the landlord for an additional 1 month’s rent." (83.575(3)). So a tenant who stays with permission gives option 4's notice when they leave. Say so. Asking the landlord for its answer in writing settles what permission there is.

## Option 3: stay without permission

Say the risk plainly. A tenant who "holds over and continues in possession of the dwelling unit or any part thereof after the expiration of the rental agreement without the permission of the landlord" (83.58) can be sued for possession (83.58), and "The landlord may also recover double the amount of rent due on the dwelling unit, or any part thereof, for the period during which the tenant refuses to surrender possession." (83.58). Do not total it. For a tenancy ended by a notice under 83.57, whether it has reached its "expiration" (83.58) is not settled. One: a tenancy ended by proper notice has expired, so double rent can apply. The other: expiration means the end of a term, and 83.57 speaks of a tenancy "terminated" (83.57).

But the end date does not put them out by itself: "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)). The landlord "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)), changing the locks included, and if it does or cuts a utility it is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months’ rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney’s fees." (83.67(6)).

What counts as permission, when the landlord said nothing or took rent for a time after the end, is not settled. One: taking rent for that time is permission, since a landlord that "accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant" (83.56(5)(a)) gives up acting on it. Then 83.58 does not apply, and 83.575(3) and option 4's notice do. The other: permission must be given, and taking rent alone does not change a tenant who holds over, since the same sentence leaves open "any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)). Set what the landlord did and any lease clause on consent beside both. Getting the landlord's answer in writing settles it either way.

## Option 4: end a tenancy with no set end date

"A tenancy without a specific duration, as defined in s. 83.46 (2) or (3), may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4)" (83.57). No reason is named. The notice, by rent period: year to year, 60 days before the end of the year's period (83.57(1)); quarter to quarter, 30 days (83.57(2)); month to month, "not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)); week to week, 7 days (83.57(4)).

1. **The last day.** Month to month: count_days(period_end, -30). If that has passed, the same notice works for the next period: count_days(next_period_end, -30). For another rent period, use its number of days.
2. **Written, and delivered a way the statute names** (see "How a notice is delivered").
3. **The 7 days' notice too.** "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (83.49(5)), it also applies to "any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year" (83.49(5)). It must be written, by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address, at least 7 days before leaving: count_days(planned_move_out, -7). Read the lease for a clause on notice before leaving. One notice by hand or certified mail, with the address, in time for both, meets both. Missing it "relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)).

A tenant who stayed on with permission after a set term and misses the 83.57(3) notice owes the extra month's rent (83.575(3)). For a tenancy that was month to month from the start, that is not settled. One: (3) names the month-to-month notice, so it applies. The other: the section is about a tenancy "with specific duration" (83.575), so it does not.

## When the landlord will not renew

The tenant has a set end date and the landlord says it will not renew. Part II names no reason it must give.

- **The lease has a notice clause with the landlord's half.** The last day for the landlord: count_days(lease_end_date, -N). If the clause is outside the limit, set the notice beside the lease's date and the limit's, as in option 1. If it is in months, give the lease's words. In a named way, on or before the last day: met, and the lease ends on its date. Say so plainly. Late, or not in a named way: what follows is not settled. One: the lease still ends on its date by its own words, and the landlord's miss is a failure of the lease, for damages at most (83.55). The other: the clause makes the landlord's notice the way a lease is not renewed, so without it the landlord cannot hold the tenant to the end date. Say what the lease says about renewal.
- **The lease has no such clause.** The stored text asks for no notice from the landlord before a set term ends. Say so plainly.
- Either way, see option 3 for staying, and "After a complaint" below.

## When the landlord ends a tenancy with no set end date

Set the landlord's notice beside option 4's rule. Month to month: count_days(period_end, -30), with period_end the last day of the rent period holding the date the notice names. If it was mailed or left at the door, use both dates, as "How a notice is delivered" says.

- **Written, in a named way, on or before that date:** met, and the tenancy ends at period_end. Say so plainly, and go to option 3 for staying.
- **Too late for that period, or naming a date that is not the end of a rent period:** it does not meet the rule for that date. Say so plainly. Whether it works for a later period is not settled. One: it is still written notice, so if it came by count_days(next_period_end, -30) the tenancy can end at next_period_end. The other: it names an end the statute does not allow, so it is not the required notice, and the landlord must give a new one.
- **By text, by portal, or spoken:** see "How a notice is delivered".

Whichever it is, say not to ignore it, and that the landlord still needs a court case (option 3).

## After a complaint

"It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Not renewing, or giving 83.57's notice, is not named there. Whether either is covered by itself is not settled. One: it is a step toward the action the rule names, so it is covered. The other: the rule lists the landlord's acts, and this is not one.

A tenant sued for possession can raise it as a defense (83.64(2)). The examples of what is protected include a complaint to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)), a tenant organization (83.64(1)(b)), and a complaint under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)), and they are only examples (83.64(1)). The tenant must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)), and "“Good faith” means honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned." (83.43(8)). They must be treated differently (83.64(4)), and the landlord must have acted primarily to retaliate, which is for a court.

It falls away "if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)), whose examples include "violation of the terms of this chapter." (83.64(3)). Whether staying after the end is that kind of violation is not settled. One: holding over without permission is what 83.58 addresses, so it is good cause. The other: that would leave the defense nothing to do whenever a lease has ended. Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## If the landlord sues

Say this first when a case has been filed. "In an action by the landlord for possession of a dwelling unit, if the tenant interposes any defense other than payment, including, but not limited to, the defense of a defective 3-day notice, the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing thereon." (83.60(2)). A motion needs papers showing why the amount is wrong (83.60(2)). A tenant with subsidized rent deposits only their own share (83.60(2)). Give the 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them; "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). The winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying a lease's notice clause binds the tenant without checking the landlord's half and the 30 to 60 days.
- Saying a tenant owes the charge for missing a notice without every condition of 83.575(2), or applying 83.595(4)'s limits to it.
- Saying the tenant must be out on the end date, or that the landlord may then remove them without a court case.
- Stating double rent as owed while what the landlord said or did leaves permission in doubt, or applying 83.575(3) with no permission.
- Applying 83.57's 30 days to a set term still running, or treating a late notice as good for the date it names.
- Saying part II gives a right to renew, or requires a reason for not renewing.
- Giving a calendar date for the 5 days in 83.60(2).
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

tool_calls.result: 83.67 Prohibited practices. — (1) A landlord of any dwelling unit governed by this part shall not cause, directly or indirectly, the termination or interruption of any utility service furnished the tenant, including, but not limited to, water, heat, light, electricity, gas, elevator, garbage collection, or refrigeration, whether or not the utility service is under the control of, or payment is made by, the landlord. (2) A landlord of any dwelling unit governed by this part shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means, including, but not limited to, changing the locks or using any bootlock or similar device. (3) A landlord of any dwelling unit governed by this part shall not discriminate against a servicemember in offering a dwelling unit for rent or in any of the terms of the rental agreement. (4) A landlord shall not prohibit a tenant from displaying one portable, removable, cloth or plastic United States flag, not larger than 4 and 1 / 2 feet by 6 feet, in a respectful manner in or on the dwelling unit regardless of any provision in the rental agreement dealing with flags or decorations. The United States flag shall be displayed in accordance with s. 83.52 (6). The landlord is not liable for damages caused by a United States flag displayed by a tenant. Any United States flag may not infringe upon the space rented by any other tenant. (5) A landlord of any dwelling unit governed by this part shall not remove the outside doors, locks, roof, walls, or windows of the unit except for purposes of maintenance, repair, or replacement; and the landlord shall not remove the tenant’s personal property from the dwelling unit unless such action is taken after surrender, abandonment, recovery of possession of the dwelling unit due to the death of the last remaining tenant in accordance with s. 83.59 (3)(d), or a lawful eviction. If provided in the rental agreement or a written agreement separate from the rental agreement, upon surrender or abandonment by the tenant, the landlord is not required to comply with s. 715.104 and is not liable or responsible for storage or disposition of the tenant’s personal property; if provided in the rental agreement, there must be printed or clearly stamped on such rental agreement a legend in substantially the following form: BY SIGNING THIS RENTAL AGREEMENT, THE TENANT AGREES THAT UPON SURRENDER, ABANDONMENT, OR RECOVERY OF POSSESSION OF THE DWELLING UNIT DUE TO THE DEATH OF THE LAST REMAINING TENANT, AS PROVIDED BY CHAPTER 83, FLORIDA STATUTES, THE LANDLORD SHALL NOT BE LIABLE OR RESPONSIBLE FOR STORAGE OR DISPOSITION OF THE TENANT’S PERSONAL PROPERTY. For the purposes of this section, abandonment shall be as set forth in s. 83.59 (3)(c). (6) A landlord who violates any provision of this section shall be liable to the tenant for actual and consequential damages or 3 months’ rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney’s fees. Subsequent or repeated violations that are not contemporaneous with the initial violation shall be subject to separate awards of damages. (7) A violation of this section constitutes irreparable harm for the purposes of injunctive relief. (8) The remedies provided by this section are not exclusive and do not preclude the tenant from pursuing any other remedy at law or equity that the tenant may have. The remedies provided by this section shall also apply to a servicemember who is a prospective tenant who has been discriminated against under subsection (3). History. — s. 3, ch. 87-369; s. 7, ch. 88-379; s. 3, ch. 90-133; s. 3, ch. 96-146; s. 2, ch. 2001-179; s. 2, ch. 2003-30; s. 4, ch. 2003-72; s. 1, ch. 2004-236; s. 2, ch. 2007-136.

Place the amount of partial rent accepted from the tenant in the registry of the court upon filing the action for possession; or 3. Post a new 3-day notice reflecting the new amount due.

(3) If the tenant remains on the premises with the permission of the landlord after the rental agreement has terminated and fails to give notice required under s. 83.57 (3), the tenant is liable to the landlord for an additional 1 month’s rent.
(3) When the tenancy is from month to month, by giving not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period; and
7. NOTICES TO LANDLORD. Written notices to Landlord shall be delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, Gainesville, Florida 32608, or sent there by certified mail.

answer:
**Short answer:** Your landlord broke the 60-day promise in your lease, but that probably doesn't stop your lease from ending on July 31. The law is not settled on what a late notice does. One reading says the lease still ends on its date and you must leave. The other says your landlord can't hold you to that date without proper notice. Either way, you shouldn't ignore the letter. Even if you stay past July 31, your landlord can't lock you out or remove you without a court case.

Do you plan to move out by July 31, or are you thinking of staying?

DETAILS

### Was your landlord's notice on time?
- Your lease, section 11, says your landlord "shall give Tenant at least 60 days' written notice, delivered as the law provides, if this lease will not be renewed."
- The last day for that notice was June 1, 2026. That date has passed.
- You told me the letter was handed to you at the apartment door on July 10. Handing it over counts as a delivery method the law names (83.56(4)). The delivery was fine, but it came after June 1.
- The 60 days also fits the statute's limit of "not less than 30 days' notice or more than 60 days' notice" (83.575(1)). Your lease also includes the landlord's half, so the clause is a kind the statute allows.

### Does the late notice mean you can stay?
This is not settled. There are two readings.
- **Reading one:** Section 3 of your lease says it "ends on July 31, 2026." The landlord's late notice breaks the lease, but the lease still ends on its date. You would at most have a damages claim against your landlord (83.55).
- **Reading two:** Section 11 makes the landlord's 60-day notice the way a non-renewal happens. Without it, the landlord can't hold you to the end date.
- The statute doesn't say which reading is right. A court would decide.

### Do you have a right to renew?
- No. Part II names no right to renew, and it doesn't require your landlord to give a reason for not renewing.
- Your lease section 9 says that if you stay after July 31, 2026 "with Landlord's written consent, the tenancy becomes month to month." Without written consent, that clause doesn't help you.

### What if you stay past July 31?
- A landlord "shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except" through a court case, or when the tenant gives up or abandons the home (83.59(3)).
- Your landlord also "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)). That includes changing the locks. If your landlord does this or cuts a utility, it can owe you "actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney's fees" (83.67(6)).
- Staying without permission is risky. If you "hold over" after the lease ends without permission, your landlord can sue you for possession. It can also seek "double the amount of rent due" for the time you refuse to leave (83.58).
- Whether double rent applies is a separate question. It depends on whether you stayed with or without permission, and on how the court reads the late notice.
- No eviction case has been filed, according to what you confirmed. If one is filed, don't ignore the court papers. Under 83.60(2), you generally must pay rent into the court registry, or file a motion about the amount, within 5 days (not counting weekends and holidays) after you are served. If you miss that, you lose most defenses.

### Could your landlord charge you the $2,100?
- Section 12 of your lease sets $2,100 in liquidated damages (a pre-set charge) if you move out at the end of the term without giving notice under section 11.
- Under 83.575(2), your landlord can charge it only after sending its own written notice. That notice must explain your notice duties, give the termination date, and "list all fees, penalties, and other charges."
- The letter you described only says the lease won't be renewed and that you must be out by July 31. It doesn't mention that charge.
- It also isn't clear that the charge applies when the landlord is the one ending the lease.

Loaded lease_ending. Its instructions:

# Lease ending

Rests on 83.575 (a set end date), 83.57 and 83.46 (no set end date), 83.58, 83.59, and 83.67 (staying on, no lockout), 83.56 and 83.505 (delivering notices), 83.49 (the 7 days' notice, the deposit), 83.595 and 83.45 (limits on charges), 83.43 and 83.64 (good faith, retaliation), 83.60 (if sued), 83.47, 83.55, and 83.48 (void clauses, damages, attorney fees), and 83.5615 (foreclosure). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes"). Every point marked not settled gets both readings, and you choose neither.

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- The tenant wants to move out well before the end date: load wants_to_leave_early.
- The landlord's notice names something the tenant did: load notice_received_violation.
- A higher rent comes with the renewal: load rent_increased too.
- After the move, the deposit: load deposit_not_returned.
- A new owner after a foreclosure says to leave: 83.5615 calls for a notice "at least 90 days before the effective date of the notice" (83.5615(2)(a)) and protects a bona fide lease's remaining term, with limits (83.5615(2)(b)). Its note says it takes effect upon the repeal of a federal act, and the stored text does not say whether that has happened; say this needs checking.

## What the lease adds

Read the whole lease, addenda included, for: the end date; any notice before leaving at the end; any notice from the landlord; any charge for missing a notice; renewal; staying after the end; how notices go; and what move-out requires. Quote each clause and cite it.

A clause that renews the lease if no notice is given: say what it says. Whether option 1's conditions for a charge reach it is not settled. One: it is a way of charging for a missed notice, so the landlord's own notice is needed first. The other: a renewal is not a charge, and 83.575(2) speaks only of liquidated damages, so the clause stands.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- lease_end_date: the date a set term ends. period_end: with no set end date, the last day of the rent period they ask about. next_period_end: the last day of the rent period after that.
- planned_move_out: the date they plan to leave.
- tenant_notice_delivered: the date their notice reached the landlord, and how it went.
- landlord_notice_delivered: the date a paper from the landlord about the end reached them, how it came, and what it lists. If mailed or left at the door, landlord_notice_sent: the date it was mailed or left.
- permission: what the landlord has said or done about their staying, and whether it is in writing. rent_after_end: any rent paid or taken for a time after the end.
- eviction_filed: whether a case has been filed, and whether they were served. complaint_date: the date of any complaint before the landlord acted, and what it was.

## Which kind of tenancy

- **A set end date:** 83.575. Options 1 to 3, and "When the landlord will not renew".
- **No set end date:** 83.57. "If the rental agreement contains no provision as to duration of the tenancy, the duration is determined by the periods for which the rent is payable." (83.46(2)). A home that comes with a job goes by the pay periods (83.46(3)). Option 4, and "When the landlord ends a tenancy with no set end date".
- **Stayed on with permission after a set term:** read the lease's clause on staying. With none, 83.575(3) points to the 83.57(3) notice; see option 2.

Part II names no right to renew.

## How a notice is delivered

This covers a landlord's notice under 83.575, and either side's notice under 83.57. A tenant's own notice before leaving at the end of a set term goes as the lease says; 83.575(1) names no way for it. The ways: "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence." (83.56(4)).

- **Handed over:** delivered that day.
- **Mailed, or left at the door while the tenant was away:** a way the statute names, but not settled which day counts. One: the mailing or the leaving is the delivery. The other: a paper is delivered when it reaches the person. For a landlord's notice, set both landlord_notice_sent and landlord_notice_delivered beside the date. For the tenant's own notice, handing it over or mailing it early meets both.
- **E-mail under the signed addendum:** only with every condition of 83.505(1); then it is "deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)).
- **A text, a portal message, an e-mail with no addendum, or a copy left at the door while the tenant was home:** not a way 83.56(4) names. Not settled whether it still counts because it reached the person. One: delivery "shall be by" (83.56(4)) the ways named, so it is not the required notice. The other: "This section does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). If there is still time, sending it again by hand or by mail meets both.
- **Spoken:** the statute asks for a written notice in these cases. No notice has been given.

A lease clause on notices adds to this: a way that meets both the clause and the statute is safest. Say what the clause says.

## Option 1: leave at the end of a set term

1. **Does the lease ask for notice?** The lease "may contain a provision requiring the tenant to notify the landlord within a specified period before vacating the premises at the end of the rental agreement" (83.575(1)). No such clause: the stored text asks for no notice before leaving on the end date. Say so plainly.
2. **Is the clause one the statute allows?** Two limits, each with its own question. Say what is not settled, and that notice by the date given meets both readings.
   - The length: "A rental agreement may not require less than 30 days’ notice or more than 60 days’ notice from either the tenant or the landlord." (83.575(1)). A clause outside it: not settled what follows. One: the statute does not rewrite such a clause, so no notice is owed under it. The other: a clause is void only "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) takes away what part II gives, so it stands at the limit. Over 60 days: the date is count_days(lease_end_date, -60). Under 30 days: count_days(lease_end_date, -30).
   - The landlord's half: the clause must also require "the landlord to notify the tenant in a manner prescribed by s. 83.56 (4) within such notice period if the rental agreement will not be renewed." (83.575(1)). A clause without it: not settled what follows. One: the statute allows the clause only "if such provision also requires" (83.575(1)) that, so no notice is owed under it. The other: the statute does not say the tenant's promise falls away, so it still binds. The date is the lease's own.
3. **The last day.** If the clause gives a number of days N: count_days(lease_end_date, -N). If it is in months, give the lease's words; the tool counts days only.

Leaving before the last day of the term: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (83.49(5)), a tenant leaving "before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement" (83.49(5)) gives the 7 days' notice: count_days(planned_move_out, -7), in writing, by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address where the tenant can be reached (83.49(5)). Read the lease for a clause on notice before leaving. Rent through the end date is still owed under the lease.

**What missing the notice costs.** A lease "may provide that if a tenant fails to give the required notice before vacating the premises at the end of the rental agreement, the tenant may be liable for liquidated damages as specified in the rental agreement" (83.575(2)). All of these must be met for that charge:

1. **The tenant missed a required notice.** They gave it in time, or the clause falls under step 2's limits: say so, with step 2's readings.
2. **The lease sets the charge.** No charge in the lease: this part does not apply.
3. **The landlord sent its own written notice first,** "specifying the tenant’s obligations under the notification provision contained in the rental agreement and the date the rental agreement is terminated." (83.575(2)), and it "must list all fees, penalties, and other charges applicable to the tenant under this subsection." (83.575(2)). No such notice, or one that leaves any of these out: not met, and the charge is not owed. Say so plainly.
4. **Delivered a way the statute names** (see "How a notice is delivered").
5. **In time.** "within 15 days before the start of the notification period contained in the rental agreement." (83.575(2)). The start: count_days(lease_end_date, -N). Fifteen days before it: count_days(lease_end_date, -(N+15)); pass the sum as one number. What the words ask is not settled. One: the notice must come during the 15 days that end when the period starts, not earlier. The other: it must come no later than 15 days before the period starts, and earlier is also in time. Set the date it came beside both dates:
   - On the earlier date: it meets both. Say so plainly.
   - Between the two: it meets only the first reading.
   - Before the earlier date: it meets only the second reading.
   - After the start: it meets neither, and the charge is not owed. Say so plainly.

The limit on fees for leaving early does not apply here: 83.595(4) "does not apply if the breach is failure to give notice as provided in s. 83.575 ." (83.595(4)(b)). Do not apply its two months' rent limit or its separate addendum to this charge. Part II sets no number for this charge; a court may refuse or limit an "unconscionable" (83.45(1)) clause, and that is for a court. Apart from this charge, a landlord may claim damages for a failure to follow the lease (83.55); amounts are outside this tool.

Moving out: read what the lease requires. Any claim on the deposit goes through the deposit steps; load deposit_not_returned after the move.

## Option 2: stay on with the landlord's agreement

A new lease or a written agreement says what the rent and the term are. Read the lease's clause on staying and what it requires. "If the tenant remains on the premises with the permission of the landlord after the rental agreement has terminated and fails to give notice required under s. 83.57 (3), the tenant is liable to the landlord for an additional 1 month’s rent." (83.575(3)). So a tenant who stays with permission gives option 4's notice when they leave. Say so. Asking the landlord for its answer in writing settles what permission there is.

## Option 3: stay without permission

Say the risk plainly. A tenant who "holds over and continues in possession of the dwelling unit or any part thereof after the expiration of the rental agreement without the permission of the landlord" (83.58) can be sued for possession (83.58), and "The landlord may also recover double the amount of rent due on the dwelling unit, or any part thereof, for the period during which the tenant refuses to surrender possession." (83.58). Do not total it. For a tenancy ended by a notice under 83.57, whether it has reached its "expiration" (83.58) is not settled. One: a tenancy ended by proper notice has expired, so double rent can apply. The other: expiration means the end of a term, and 83.57 speaks of a tenancy "terminated" (83.57).

But the end date does not put them out by itself: "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)). The landlord "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)), changing the locks included, and if it does or cuts a utility it is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months’ rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney’s fees." (83.67(6)).

What counts as permission, when the landlord said nothing or took rent for a time after the end, is not settled. One: taking rent for that time is permission, since a landlord that "accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant" (83.56(5)(a)) gives up acting on it. Then 83.58 does not apply, and 83.575(3) and option 4's notice do. The other: permission must be given, and taking rent alone does not change a tenant who holds over, since the same sentence leaves open "any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)). Set what the landlord did and any lease clause on consent beside both. Getting the landlord's answer in writing settles it either way.

## Option 4: end a tenancy with no set end date

"A tenancy without a specific duration, as defined in s. 83.46 (2) or (3), may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4)" (83.57). No reason is named. The notice, by rent period: year to year, 60 days before the end of the year's period (83.57(1)); quarter to quarter, 30 days (83.57(2)); month to month, "not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)); week to week, 7 days (83.57(4)).

1. **The last day.** Month to month: count_days(period_end, -30). If that has passed, the same notice works for the next period: count_days(next_period_end, -30). For another rent period, use its number of days.
2. **Written, and delivered a way the statute names** (see "How a notice is delivered").
3. **The 7 days' notice too.** "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (83.49(5)), it also applies to "any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year" (83.49(5)). It must be written, by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address, at least 7 days before leaving: count_days(planned_move_out, -7). Read the lease for a clause on notice before leaving. One notice by hand or certified mail, with the address, in time for both, meets both. Missing it "relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)).

A tenant who stayed on with permission after a set term and misses the 83.57(3) notice owes the extra month's rent (83.575(3)). For a tenancy that was month to month from the start, that is not settled. One: (3) names the month-to-month notice, so it applies. The other: the section is about a tenancy "with specific duration" (83.575), so it does not.

## When the landlord will not renew

The tenant has a set end date and the landlord says it will not renew. Part II names no reason it must give.

- **The lease has a notice clause with the landlord's half.** The last day for the landlord: count_days(lease_end_date, -N). If the clause is outside the limit, set the notice beside the lease's date and the limit's, as in option 1. If it is in months, give the lease's words. In a named way, on or before the last day: met, and the lease ends on its date. Say so plainly. Late, or not in a named way: what follows is not settled. One: the lease still ends on its date by its own words, and the landlord's miss is a failure of the lease, for damages at most (83.55). The other: the clause makes the landlord's notice the way a lease is not renewed, so without it the landlord cannot hold the tenant to the end date. Say what the lease says about renewal.
- **The lease has no such clause.** The stored text asks for no notice from the landlord before a set term ends. Say so plainly.
- Either way, see option 3 for staying, and "After a complaint" below.

## When the landlord ends a tenancy with no set end date

Set the landlord's notice beside option 4's rule. Month to month: count_days(period_end, -30), with period_end the last day of the rent period holding the date the notice names. If it was mailed or left at the door, use both dates, as "How a notice is delivered" says.

- **Written, in a named way, on or before that date:** met, and the tenancy ends at period_end. Say so plainly, and go to option 3 for staying.
- **Too late for that period, or naming a date that is not the end of a rent period:** it does not meet the rule for that date. Say so plainly. Whether it works for a later period is not settled. One: it is still written notice, so if it came by count_days(next_period_end, -30) the tenancy can end at next_period_end. The other: it names an end the statute does not allow, so it is not the required notice, and the landlord must give a new one.
- **By text, by portal, or spoken:** see "How a notice is delivered".

Whichever it is, say not to ignore it, and that the landlord still needs a court case (option 3).

## After a complaint

"It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Not renewing, or giving 83.57's notice, is not named there. Whether either is covered by itself is not settled. One: it is a step toward the action the rule names, so it is covered. The other: the rule lists the landlord's acts, and this is not one.

A tenant sued for possession can raise it as a defense (83.64(2)). The examples of what is protected include a complaint to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)), a tenant organization (83.64(1)(b)), and a complaint under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)), and they are only examples (83.64(1)). The tenant must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)), and "“Good faith” means honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned." (83.43(8)). They must be treated differently (83.64(4)), and the landlord must have acted primarily to retaliate, which is for a court.

It falls away "if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)), whose examples include "violation of the terms of this chapter." (83.64(3)). Whether staying after the end is that kind of violation is not settled. One: holding over without permission is what 83.58 addresses, so it is good cause. The other: that would leave the defense nothing to do whenever a lease has ended. Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## If the landlord sues

Say this first when a case has been filed. "In an action by the landlord for possession of a dwelling unit, if the tenant interposes any defense other than payment, including, but not limited to, the defense of a defective 3-day notice, the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing thereon." (83.60(2)). A motion needs papers showing why the amount is wrong (83.60(2)). A tenant with subsidized rent deposits only their own share (83.60(2)). Give the 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them; "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). The winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying a lease's notice clause binds the tenant without checking the landlord's half and the 30 to 60 days.
- Saying a tenant owes the charge for missing a notice without every condition of 83.575(2), or applying 83.595(4)'s limits to it.
- Saying the tenant must be out on the end date, or that the landlord may then remove them without a court case.
- Stating double rent as owed while what the landlord said or did leaves permission in doubt, or applying 83.575(3) with no permission.
- Applying 83.57's 30 days to a set term still running, or treating a late notice as good for the date it names.
- Saying part II gives a right to renew, or requires a reason for not renewing.
- Giving a calendar date for the 5 days in 83.60(2).
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

(2) A rental agreement with a specific duration may provide that if a tenant fails to give the required notice before vacating the premises at the end of the rental agreement, the tenant may be liable for liquidated damages as specified in the rental agreement if the landlord provides written notice to the tenant specifying the tenant’s obligations under the notification provision contained in the rental agreement and the date the rental agreement is terminated. The landlord must provide such written notice to the tenant in a manner prescribed by s. 83.56 (4) within 15 days before the start of the notification period contained in the rental agreement. The written notice must list all fees, penalties, and other charges applicable to the tenant under this subsection. (3) If the tenant remains on the premises with the permission of the landlord after the rental agreement has terminated and fails to give notice required under s. 83.57 (3), the tenant is liable to the landlord for an additional 1 month’s rent. History. — s. 3, ch. 2003-30; s. 1, ch. 2004-375; s. 9, ch. 2013-136; s. 3, ch. 2023-314; s. 6, ch. 2025-16.

(6) A landlord who violates any provision of this section shall be liable to the tenant for actual and consequential damages or 3 months’ rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney’s fees. Subsequent or repeated violations that are not contemporaneous with the initial violation shall be subject to separate awards of damages.

83.58 Remedies; tenant holding over. — If the tenant holds over and continues in possession of the dwelling unit or any part thereof after the expiration of the rental agreement without the permission of the landlord, the landlord may recover possession of the dwelling unit in the manner provided for in s. 83.59 . The landlord may also recover double the amount of rent due on the dwelling unit, or any part thereof, for the period during which the tenant refuses to surrender possession.

(2) In an action by the landlord for possession of a dwelling unit, if the tenant interposes any defense other than payment, including, but not limited to, the defense of a defective 3-day notice, the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due. The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons. Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing thereon. If a motion to determine rent is filed, documentation in support of the allegation that the rent as alleged in the complaint is in error is required. Public housing tenants or tenants receiving rent subsidies are required to deposit only that portion of the full rent for which they are responsible pursuant to the federal, state, or local program in which they are participating.

(2) A rental agreement with a specific duration may provide that if a tenant fails to give the required notice before vacating the premises at the end of the rental agreement, the tenant may be liable for liquidated damages as specified in the rental agreement if the landlord provides written notice to the tenant specifying the tenant’s obligations under the notification provision contained in the rental agreement and the date the rental agreement is terminated. The landlord must provide such written notice to the tenant in a manner prescribed by s. 83.56 (4) within 15 days before the start of the notification period contained in the rental agreement. The written notice must list all fees, penalties, and other charges applicable to the tenant under this subsection.

11. NOTICE AT THE END OF THE TERM. Tenant shall give Landlord at least 60 days' written notice before moving out at the end of the term. Landlord shall give Tenant at least 60 days' written notice, delivered as the law provides, if this lease will not be renewed.
3. TERM. This lease begins on August 1, 2025 and ends on July 31, 2026.
9. HOLDING OVER. If Tenant stays after July 31, 2026 with Landlord's written consent, the tenancy becomes month to month on the same terms.

12. FAILURE TO GIVE NOTICE. If Tenant moves out at the end of the term without giving the notice in section 11, Tenant shall pay Landlord $2,100.00 as liquidated damages.

Landlord: Marsh Creek Property Management, LLC, by Dana Ortiz, Property Manager    Date: July 10, 2025
Tenant: Jordan Reyes    Date: July 10, 2025

answer:
**Short answer:** Your landlord can't make you leave in 5 days just by handing you that letter. The landlord would have to file a court case to remove you, and a letter isn't a court order. Whether you could owe double rent is not settled. It turns on whether the landlord accepting your August rent counts as permission to stay. If it does, the double-rent rule doesn't apply. If it doesn't, you could owe double rent, but only if the landlord wins in court. Don't ignore the letter.

Do you plan to move out, and if so, on what date?

DETAILS

### Can the landlord remove you after 5 days?
- No. The landlord "shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" through a court case, or when the tenant gives up or abandons the home (83.59(3)).
- The landlord also "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)). That covers changing the locks.
- If the landlord does this or shuts off a utility, it is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney's fees." (83.67(6)).
- You told me no eviction case has been filed.

### Does double rent apply to you?
This is not settled. Two readings:
- **Reading 1: taking your rent was permission.** A landlord that "accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant" gives up acting on it (83.56(5)(a)). On this reading, 83.58 (the double-rent rule) doesn't apply, because it covers only a tenant who stays "without the permission of the landlord." Instead, 83.575(3) applies. It makes a tenant who stays with permission and doesn't give the month-to-month notice in 83.57(3) liable for "an additional 1 month's rent."
- **Reading 2: taking rent alone is not permission.** The same subsection leaves open "any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." On this reading, you held over without permission. Section 83.58 then lets the landlord sue for possession and also recover "double the amount of rent due on the dwelling unit, or any part thereof, for the period during which the tenant refuses to surrender possession."
- Your lease supports Reading 2 somewhat. Section 9 says that if you stay after July 31 "with Landlord's written consent," the tenancy becomes month to month. You have no written consent. Section 10 says the lease may be changed only in a signed writing.
- Your facts support Reading 1. The landlord took your August rent through the portal and said nothing.
- If you want certainty, ask the landlord in writing whether you may stay. The answer would settle which reading applies.

### Does the letter work as a notice to end a month-to-month tenancy?
- If you are treated as staying with permission, the tenancy would end by written notice under 83.57(3). That notice needs "not less than 30 days' notice prior to the end of any monthly period."
- The last day to give that notice for the period ending August 31 was August 1. Your letter came August 20, so it is too late for that period.
- For the period ending September 30, the last day is August 31, and that date has not passed. Whether a late notice carries over to the next period is not settled:
  - **One reading:** the letter is still written notice, so the tenancy could end September 30.
  - **Other reading:** the letter names a 5-day deadline, which the statute doesn't allow, so it is not the required notice and the landlord must send a new one.
- The letter does not name September 30 or any end of a rent period. It says only "5 days."

### Was the letter delivered properly?
- Handing you a true copy is a delivery method the statute names (83.56(4)).
- Your lease, section 8, says notices to you "shall be delivered to the apartment while Tenant lives there." The letter was handed to you at the office instead. Your lease and the statute don't line up on that point.
- You received the letter in either case, so it is not safe to ignore.

### What would change this answer?
- **A court filing:** if you are served with a case, you would have only 5 days, not counting weekends and holidays, to pay rent into the court registry or file a motion about the amount (83.60(2)). Missing that deadline waives your defenses other than payment.
- **Your move-out date:** if you leave, a written notice by hand or certified mail with your address is due at least 7 days before you go (83.49(5)). Your lease has no different rule on that. Your lease section 6 also asks for your forwarding address in writing.
